strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem: KV cache memory overhead for long-CoT reasoning LLMs, which is increasingly important as reasoning models generate very long outputs.

Three well-motivated technical components (progressive quantization, block-wise memory allocation via Integer Programming, calibration with positional interpolation) directly target the two identified failure modes (cumulative error and short-context calibration mismatch).

Rigorous mathematical proof (Appendix D) establishing the equivalence of the proposed 'Equivalent Right Shift' bit-shrinking operation to dequantize-then-requantize, which supports the correctness of the core algorithmic trick.

Extensive experiments across a wide range of model scales (7B to 70B) and multiple reasoning/coding benchmarks (AIME-2024/2025, CMIMC, LiveCodeBench), plus additional non-reasoning (IFEval) and sparse-attention (QuestAttention) evaluations in the appendix.
Reasonably thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each component (bit-shrinking strategy, block sensitivity, positional interpolation length/scaling factor).

Comparisons against multiple relevant baselines (KIVI, RotateKV, MiKV, KVTuner) under matched hardware/batch-size constraints, and efficiency (throughput) measurements demonstrating practical speedups over 16-bit inference.
Code release and detailed experimental configuration aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited fundamental novelty: progressive/mixed-precision quantization and positional-interpolation-based calibration are combinations/adaptations of existing techniques (PI from Chen et al. 2023, mixed-precision allocation similar to prior LLM/diffusion quantization work) rather than fundamentally new ideas.

PM-KVQ's throughput is consistently *worse* than KIVI (2.45–16.18% lower per the paper's own numbers); the headline throughput gains (2.73–5.18x) are relative to unquantized 16-bit models, not to the strongest quantization baseline, which somewhat overstates the efficiency contribution.

The practical mechanics of progressive quantization in a batched-serving setting (sequences of different lengths reaching different bit-width transition points simultaneously) are not clearly explained or evaluated at scale, raising reproducibility/implementation-complexity concerns.

Method explicitly does not support Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), which is used by the actual DeepSeek-R1 model (only tested on distilled GQA-based variants), limiting applicability to the most relevant production model.

Block-wise memory allocation is evaluated with only two candidate bit-widths per model (e.g., {2,4} or {4,8}), which is a fairly coarse mixed-precision granularity and may understate/overstate the real benefit of the IP-based allocation approach.

The improvement from positional interpolation alone is modest (~1.66% pass@1 in the reported ablation), and no fair comparison is given against simply calibrating with equally long non-interpolated sequences under matched compute budget for larger models.

Statistical rigor is limited: AIME datasets have only 30 problems per year, and while means and std are reported, no significance testing is done to confirm that reported gains (some quite small, e.g., <1%) are meaningful versus noise.

The specific batch-size choices used to showcase progressive quantization/block-wise allocation benefits appear selected to create underutilized-memory scenarios; it is unclear how consistently these benefits materialize across a broader range of real-world deployment configurations beyond the two hand-picked batch sizes per model shown in Section C.5.
